newsitem.title: USA: Dollar edges higher against the mark and yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar edges higher against the mark and yen.

text.p: The dollar ended higher against the yen on Thursday after Japan reported a smaller-than-expected rise in its politically-sensitive trade surplus.
The dollar also rose modestly against the mark on growing doubts about Germany's willingness and ability to reverse recent weakness in its currency.

On Thursday, Hans Tietmeyer, the president of Germany's central bank, said he hoped the current upward "correction" of the dollar against the mark would not go too far and warned that officials were watching developments in the foreign exchange market closely.

But currency traders, who have been anticipating central bank intervention or more blunt verbal warnings to reverse mark weakness all week, took the remarks as a green light to push the dollar higher.

"The market expects them to talk the dollar down at this point," said Kevin Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh. "But the Germans just don't seem too disturbed by the current level."
The dollar ended at 1.7937 marks, up from 1.7906 on Wednesday. It also rose to 116.03 yen from 115.52.
The dollar's gains against the yen were made during Tokyo trading hours after Japan's Ministry of Finance reported solid but well contained gains in the country's June trade surplus.

The data showed that the surplus rose by 27.7 percent from a year earlier to 934.21 billion yen ($8.05 billion) while its bilateral surplus with the United States climbed 26.8 percent to 373.14 billion yen ($3.21 billion).

Although officials in Japan and the U.S. have said that they will not use currencies as a trade tool, the smaller-than-expected rise in the surplus relieved fears that trade tensions, and pressure to push the dollar lower to give U.S. exporters an advantage, would soon develop.

"The Japanese surplus went up handily. However, the market was anticipating a much larger increase and it was a buyer of dollars and seller of yen on the news," said Susan Stearns, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal.
Also supportive of the dollar on Thursday was more good news on the U.S. economy.

The Philadelphia Federal Reserve reported that its July business index, a key indicator of activity in the manufacturing sector, rose to 28.1 in July, up from 25.2 in June, and much higher than the market had expected.

Keeping dollar gains in check, dealers said, was unconfirmed but continuous talk throughout the day that European central banks were intervening to support the ailing mark, which fell to its lowest level against the dollar in six years earlier this week.
In other trade on Thursday, the dollar rose to 1.4805 Swiss francs from 1.4750 on Wednesday, and pushed up to Canadian $1.3768 from C$1.3743.
The pound fell to $1.6725 from $1.6787 on Wednesday.
